text: RF and US optimally integrated between conduction and convection cycles is considered a potentially viable approach to improve drying on the paper machine. Results from periodic application of RFUS with 500 W RF for 2 s and 120 W US for 1 s in conjunction with multi-cylinder drying for a 300 GSM sheet are shown in Figures 16 – 17. This application resulted in greater than 40% increase in overall average drying rate and drying time (Figures 16 – 17). These results confirmed the benefits of RFUS technology with uniform volumetric heating and water removal resulting in increased drying rates during the entire drying periods including the falling rate period and shorter falling rate period. 24 DE-EE0009395 Figure 16. Sheet moisture ration vs drying time for intermittent RFUS (500W RF 2s 120W US 1s) application Further optimization of RFUS with intermittent application after every conduction and convection (500 W RF for 2 s and 120 W US for 1 s) resulted in even better performance with >40% improvement in drying rate and drying time with heaviest paper grade of 300 GSM. These results clearly showed that with optimum integration of RFUS at various locations on the paper machine, desired target improvements in drying rate and drying time achieving the project goals. Modeling and simulation of the paper drying process including the integration of auxiliary energy Basic description of the paper drying transport model considering the mass, energy and momentum transport with associated governing equations, initial and boundary conditions was 25 DE-EE0009395 completed. The mathematical model is solved using multi-physics, computational simulation approaches. First the results from one sided drying of paper with hot surface on one side and air flow on the other side were simulated. [Huang, et al 2022] Then the simulation results from multi-cylinder drying of paper and board with alternating contact on either side of the sheet and pocket ventilation in the pockets between the cylinders were conducted. The cylinder temperature, pocket ventilation air temperature as well as the air velocity and humidity can be changed depending on the paper machine conditions. This model was then used to simulate commercial paper machines manufacturing liner board, corrugating medium and packaging board. The model results on the overall average drying were then compared with limited commercial machine data shared by our industry partners and the literature. The distribution of temperature, pressure and saturation inside the sheet at various points within a cylinder-draw-cylinder cycle on the paper machine dryer section is shown in Figures 18, 19 and 20. These results were obtained using a commercial linerboard machine conditions with three sections operating at varying temperatures. It is interesting to note the heating up of the sheet on one side when it is in contact with the cylinder and then cooling of the sheet in the draw or pockets and then heating up of the sheet on the other side of the sheet.
